title: Systematic, zero and random errors

learning_outcomes.text: understand and explain the effects of systematic errors, including zero errors, and random errors in measurements

prior_knowledge_summary: A physical quantity is reported with a magnitude and a unit.
Plausible estimates can be used to challenge unreasonable measurements.
SI prefixes and base-unit powers can be used to compare quantities and check a supplied equation.
Matching units are necessary but do not prove that a physical model is correct.
new_learning: A systematic error shifts repeated measurements consistently in the same direction.
A zero error is a systematic error revealed when an instrument gives a non-zero reading for a true zero input.
A random error changes unpredictably between readings and produces scatter.
Repeated readings and a mean can reduce the effect of random error, but repetition alone does not remove a systematic offset.
not_yet_taught: Applications belonging to later Physics topics.

visual_planning.reason: Six visuals establish the opening contradiction, separate offset from scatter, show a zero check and correction, model repeat-and-average reasoning, compare remedies and support a complete measurement procedure.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: How can many careful readings all be wrong?
content: Two groups measure the same reference mass. Group A obtains 50.31 g, 50.30 g, 50.32 g and 50.31 g. Group B obtains 50.02 g, 49.97 g, 50.04 g and 49.99 g. The reference value is 50.00 g.
Group A has very little variation, yet every value is too high. Group B has values on both sides of the reference. Repetition alone has exposed two different kinds of measurement problem.
We need to ask two questions. Do all readings move together in one direction, or do they vary unpredictably from one reading to the next?

figure.purpose: Create the opening contradiction by contrasting a consistent offset with two-sided scatter
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with a central 50.00 g reference line. Place four tightly grouped blue marks near 50.31 g and four orange marks scattered around 50.00 g. Label only group A, group B and reference. Do not name the error types.
figure.alt_text: One group of readings lies tightly above a reference value while another group scatters on both sides of it.

blocks.title: A fault that moves every reading together
content: Definition to learn: a systematic error is an error that causes measurements to be consistently offset from the true value in the same direction.
Imagine a balance whose scale is shifted upward by 0.30 g. A true mass of 20.00 g is shown as about 20.30 g. A true mass of 45.00 g is shown as about 45.30 g. The bias follows every measurement.

Taking more readings may make the repeated values look stable, but their shared offset remains. The scientific response is to find and correct the cause, for example by checking zero, recalibrating the instrument or comparing it with a known reference.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: an error that causes measurements to be consistently offset from the true value in the same direction

figure.purpose: Show that the same calibration shift follows different true values
figure.brief: Create a colourful hand-drawn two-row balance comparison. In each row show a true value card, a fixed +0.30 g offset arrow and the displayed value. Use 20.00 g to 20.30 g and 45.00 g to 45.30 g. Add a brace labelled same direction.
figure.alt_text: Two different true masses are both displayed 0.30 grams too high by the same balance.

blocks.title: Zero error is a special systematic error
content: Before an object is placed on a balance, the true input is zero. Suppose the empty balance reads +0.08 g. That non-zero reading at true zero is a zero error.
Because the instrument already adds 0.08 g, an indicated reading of 12.64 g must be corrected by subtracting the observed zero reading: 12.64 g - 0.08 g = 12.56 g.
Check the direction. The balance started too high, so the corrected result must be lower than the indicated reading. This reasoned direction check is independent of the subtraction.
If the empty instrument had displayed a negative value, subtracting that negative zero reading would increase the corrected result. Record the sign of the zero reading before correcting.

figure.purpose: Make a positive zero check and signed correction visible as one procedure
figure.brief: Draw a rectangular annotated balance sequence: empty pan reads +0.08 g, object on pan reads 12.64 g, correction strip shows 12.64 g minus (+0.08 g), final card 12.56 g. Use a red offset arrow and a green correction arrow. Keep the arithmetic fully visible.
figure.alt_text: An empty balance reads plus 0.08 grams and this signed zero reading is subtracted from an indicated 12.64 grams.

blocks.title: A variation that changes from reading to reading
content: Definition to learn: a random error is an unpredictable variation in repeated measurements that causes readings to scatter about the true value.
A student times the same regular event several times and obtains 2.41 s, 2.35 s, 2.39 s, 2.43 s and 2.37 s. Small changes in the start and stop judgement can move one reading up and another down.
The mean is (2.41 + 2.35 + 2.39 + 2.43 + 2.37) s / 5 = 2.39 s. Positive and negative variations partly cancel in the mean.
Repeating only once is weak evidence. Several independent readings reveal the scatter and make the mean less sensitive to one unusually high or low value.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: an unpredictable variation in repeated measurements that causes readings to scatter about the true value

figure.purpose: Connect two-sided scatter to the repeat-and-mean response
figure.brief: Create a hand-drawn number-line sequence for five time readings from 2.35 s to 2.43 s. Mark their mean at 2.39 s in a contrasting colour. Add small arrows from the five readings into a mean box, without using later-lesson vocabulary.
figure.alt_text: Five time readings scatter around a mean of 2.39 seconds and feed into a mean calculation.

blocks.title: More readings do not cure every error
content: It feels reasonable that enough measurements must reveal the correct value. That idea works only when the variations change direction and can partly cancel.
If every reading contains the same +0.30 g offset, their mean also contains +0.30 g. Averaging a systematic error preserves the bias. A zero check, calibration or method change is needed.

For random error, repeat under the same intended conditions and calculate a mean. For a changing object, also measure at sensible different positions or orientations when the goal is to represent the whole object.
The remedy must match the pattern: diagnose and correct a shared cause for a systematic error; repeat and average for random variation.

figure.purpose: Contrast the correct response to a shared offset with the correct response to random scatter
figure.brief: Draw a two-column teacher decision card. Left: readings all shifted right, leading to check zero, calibrate or change method. Right: readings scattered on both sides, leading to repeat and mean. Cross out an arrow from repeat and mean to removal of the shared offset.
figure.alt_text: A decision card assigns calibration to a shared offset and repetition with a mean to random scatter.

blocks.title: Plan a trustworthy wire measurement
content: A wire diameter is too small for a metre rule. A micrometer screw gauge is a suitable instrument for this small dimension. Before measuring, close it gently and inspect the zero reading.
Suppose the closed micrometer reads +0.03 mm. Record this signed zero error. If a wire reading is 0.57 mm, the corrected diameter is 0.57 mm - 0.03 mm = 0.54 mm.

One location may not represent the whole wire. Take readings at several positions and turn the wire so that more than one diameter is sampled. Correct each reading for the same zero error, then calculate the mean of the corrected readings.
The zero correction addresses a systematic offset. The spread from position, orientation and reading judgement is handled by repeated sampling and a mean. These are separate jobs.

figure.purpose: Integrate instrument selection, zero checking, multiple positions and rotation into one procedure
figure.brief: Create a rectangular colourful hand-drawn procedure strip. Show a closed micrometer with +0.03 mm, a wire marked at three separated positions, a small rotation arrow at each position and a final mean box. Use numbered arrows. Do not introduce uncertainty notation or later-lesson terms.
figure.alt_text: A measurement procedure checks the micrometer zero, samples several wire positions and orientations, corrects readings and calculates a mean.

blocks.title: Read the pattern before choosing the remedy
content: First inspect the instrument at a known input, especially true zero. A non-zero reading at zero identifies a zero error and gives a signed correction.
Next take repeated readings. A consistent shift in the same direction points to a systematic cause. Unpredictable variation from reading to reading points to random error.

Then act on the cause. Correct, recalibrate or replace a method that gives a systematic offset. Repeat and average when random variation is present. Many real measurements contain both effects, so the two actions may both be needed.
Keep the language narrow. This lesson diagnoses error patterns and chooses responses. The next lesson will introduce the separate ideas of precision, accuracy and resolution.

concepts_taught: systematic error as a consistent same-direction offset
zero error as a systematic offset revealed at true zero
random error as unpredictable scatter between repeated readings
different remedies for systematic and random errors
misconceptions_addressed: closely grouped readings must be free from error
taking more readings removes a systematic offset
one measurement location is always representative of an object
skills_students_can_now_use: distinguish a consistent offset from unpredictable scatter
identify a zero error from an instrument's reading at true zero
apply a signed zero correction to an indicated reading
reduce the effect of random error using repeated readings and a mean
select a suitable small-dimension instrument and plan repeated sampling
next_lesson_can_assume: the controlled meanings of systematic error and random error
zero error is a systematic error and can be corrected using its signed reading
averaging reduces random scatter but does not remove a systematic offset
next_lesson_must_not_assume: the controlled meanings of precision, accuracy or instrument resolution
